questions.stem: Which component makes up over half of blood's volume?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Red cells claim most of the remaining half.
White cells are a small fraction.
Platelets are the smallest share.

questions.stem: Which structural feature do red blood cells lack?

options.explanation: That is the shape they have.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Every cell keeps its membrane.
Haemoglobin is precisely what they contain.

questions.stem: Which component consists of cell fragments?

options.explanation: Plasma is the fluid, not a fragment.
Those are whole white cells.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
They are whole, if unusual, cells.

questions.stem: How are white blood cells described in the composition table?

options.explanation: That is the red cell description.
That describes plasma.
That describes platelets.

options.text: Large cells containing a large nucleus, with differing types and functions
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: What colour and form is plasma?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Red comes from the cells, not the carrier.
Plasma is liquid.
It is an aqueous solution, not oil.

questions.stem: List the four components of blood.
questions.modelAnswer: Red cells, white cells, platelets, and the plasma that carries them.

questions.stem: Describe the structure of a red blood cell.
questions.modelAnswer: A biconcave disc with no nucleus, containing haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Explain why blood is described as a suspension rather than a simple solution.
questions.modelAnswer: Because whole cells and fragments are held dispersed in the plasma liquid, rather than dissolved into it as solutes would be.

questions.stem: A centrifuge spins a sample and separates layers. Predict the arrangement.
questions.modelAnswer: Dense red cells pack at the bottom, white cells and platelets form a thin middle layer, and straw-coloured plasma sits on top.

questions.stem: Where does plasma take carbon dioxide?

options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is not stored anywhere.

options.text: From the respiring cells to the lungs
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: From the lungs to the cells
options.explanation: The flow of carbon dioxide runs the other way.
Urea goes to the kidneys; carbon dioxide goes to the lungs.

questions.stem: Which plasma cargo heads for the kidneys?

options.explanation: Hormones head for their target tissues.
Food heads for the cells that need it.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Oxygen goes to respiring cells.

questions.stem: What are hormones in the plasma?

options.text: Waste products bound for the lungs
options.explanation: Hormones are signals, not wastes.
Digestion products are food cargo.
That is haemoglobin's role in the red cells.

options.text: Chemical messengers released by glands and delivered to target organs
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: How does plasma help control body temperature?

options.text: It carries heat energy to cooler regions or to the skin where it can be lost
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Cooling comes from heat transfer, not freezing.
It redistributes heat rather than blocking it.
Generation happens in respiration; plasma only transports.

questions.stem: Which cargo is absorbed from the small intestine into the plasma?

options.explanation: Antibodies come from lymphocytes, not digestion.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Urea is collected after liver action, not from the gut's absorption.
Carbon dioxide loads at the cells.

questions.stem: List the five cargoes plasma transports.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, digested food, mineral ions, urea, hormones and heat energy.

questions.stem: State where digested food is loaded into the plasma.
questions.modelAnswer: Dissolved particles are absorbed from the small intestine.

questions.stem: Explain why plasma's watery nature suits its transport role.
questions.modelAnswer: Because water dissolves ions, sugars, urea and carbon dioxide readily, so one carrier liquid can serve every organ without switching vehicles.

questions.stem: After a protein-rich meal, name the plasma cargo that rises and its destination.
questions.modelAnswer: Digested food rises — amino acids absorbed from the small intestine — travelling to cells that need material for growth and repair.

questions.stem: What does haemoglobin do in a red blood cell?

options.explanation: Clotting uses fibrin, not haemoglobin.
Urea rides the plasma.

options.text: It binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is phagocyte work.

questions.stem: Why is the absence of a nucleus an advantage for a red cell?

options.text: It lets the cell divide faster
options.explanation: Red cells do not divide.

options.text: It makes the cell lighter to float
options.explanation: Buoyancy is irrelevant.

options.text: It allows oxygen through the membrane
options.explanation: Diffusion happens at the membrane regardless.

options.text: It leaves more space to pack in haemoglobin
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: What shape is a red blood cell?

options.text: A biconcave disc, dented inward toward its middle
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
No square shapes exist in blood.
That resembles a vessel, not a cell.
The dimple is the defining feature.

questions.stem: What advantage does the biconcave shape give?

options.explanation: Speed comes from blood flow, not cell shape.

options.text: A larger surface-area-to-volume ratio for fast oxygen diffusion
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Shape is not armour here.
There is no nucleus.

questions.stem: To which cells do red blood cells deliver their cargo?

options.explanation: The brain is one customer among all.
Muscles are heavy users, not the only users.

options.text: Every respiring cell in the body
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The lungs load the oxygen; delivery is body-wide.

questions.stem: Name the oxygen-binding protein in red blood cells.
State the three adaptations of red blood cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Packed haemoglobin, no nucleus, and a biconcave disc shape.

questions.stem: Explain why the three red-cell adaptations function as a set.
questions.modelAnswer: Because haemoglobin provides the binding chemistry, the missing nucleus provides the packing space for it, and the biconcave shape speeds the gas across the membrane — delivery depends on all three.

questions.stem: At altitude, the body makes more red cells. Explain the benefit using their adaptations.
questions.modelAnswer: More red cells means more total haemoglobin per litre, so the thinner-air oxygen still gets bound and delivered despite the lower partial pressure.
